draft.title: VA DIC Claims & Survivor Benefits Assistance
draft.excerpt: Dependency and Indemnity Compensation provides a monthly, tax-free payment to surviving spouses and dependents when a veteran’s death is service-connected. We help survivors establish the connection and navigate the claims process.
draft.body:
What Is DIC?

Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (DIC) is a monthly, tax-free benefit paid by the VA to surviving spouses, children, and dependent parents of veterans whose deaths were service-connected , or who, at the time of death, were rated totally disabled by the VA for a specified period of time.

DIC is not a one-time payment; it is an ongoing monthly benefit. The base rate for a surviving spouse (without other additions) is set by Congress and adjusted periodically. Additional amounts may be available for dependent children, for Aid and Attendance needs, and in other circumstances.

Who May Qualify

  • Surviving spouse , married to the veteran at the time of death and meeting continuous cohabitation requirements
  • Surviving children , unmarried children under 18, or under 23 if in school, or permanently disabled before age 18
  • Dependent parents , may qualify for a separate benefit based on the veteran’s service-connected death

Paths to Service Connection for the Cause of Death

The central question in most DIC claims is whether the veteran’s death was caused by, or substantially contributed to by, a service-connected or service-connectable condition. This analysis can be complex. The paths include:

  • Direct service connection , the condition that caused death began during or was aggravated by active duty service
  • Secondary service connection , the cause of death was caused or aggravated by an already service-connected condition
  • The 10-year presumption , if the veteran had a continuous total rating for 10 or more years before death, the surviving spouse may be entitled regardless of cause of death
  • The 5-year presumption , a total rating in place for 5 or more years immediately before death, where the condition could not have improved, may also qualify
  • Ratings before death , if the veteran had a claim pending at the time of death, the surviving spouse may be able to substitute for the veteran and continue pursuing that claim

Substitution and Pending Claims

When a veteran dies while a VA claim or appeal is pending, an eligible survivor may apply to substitute for the veteran within one year of the veteran’s death. Substitution allows the survivor to step into the veteran’s shoes and pursue the claim to a final decision, potentially securing retroactive benefits that accrue back to the original filing date.

This is a time-sensitive right. Missing the one-year substitution deadline extinguishes it. If the veteran had a pending claim when they passed, contact us promptly.

For more information about eligibility requirements, benefits and how to apply, visit the official VA Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (DIC) guide.

  • Direct service connection , the condition that caused death began during or was aggravated by active duty service
  • Secondary service connection , the cause of death was caused or aggravated by an already service-connected condition
  • The 10-year presumption , if the veteran had a continuous total rating for 10 or more years before death, the surviving spouse may be entitled regardless of cause of death
  • The 5-year presumption , a total rating in place for 5 or more years immediately before death, where the condition could not have improved, may also qualify
  • Ratings before death , if the veteran had a claim pending at the time of death, the surviving spouse may be able to substitute for the veteran and continue pursuing that claim

Substitution and Pending Claims

When a veteran dies while a VA claim or appeal is pending, an eligible survivor may apply to substitute for the veteran within one year of the veteran’s death. Substitution allows the survivor to step into the veteran’s shoes and pursue the claim to a final decision , potentially securing retroactive benefits that accrue back to the original filing date.

This is a time-sensitive right. Missing the one-year substitution deadline extinguishes it. If the veteran had a pending claim when they passed, contact us promptly.

draft.title: Discharge Upgrades
draft.excerpt: A less-than-honorable discharge can bar a veteran from VA benefits, employment, and more. We assist veterans in petitioning for character of discharge upgrades before the Discharge Review Boards and Boards for Correction of Military Records.
draft.body:
Why Discharge Character Matters

The character of a veteran’s discharge , Honorable, General (Under Honorable Conditions), Other Than Honorable (OTH), Bad Conduct, or Dishonorable , determines eligibility for most VA benefits. A veteran discharged OTH or worse may be barred from VA health care, disability compensation, education benefits, and other programs that would otherwise be available based on their service.

For some veterans, the discharge characterization reflects circumstances that were shaped by untreated mental health conditions, military sexual trauma, or situations involving systemic error or injustice. The upgrade process exists to address those cases.

Available Forums

  • Discharge Review Board (DRB) each military branch has a DRB that can review discharges within 15 years of the separation date; can change character of discharge and reason for discharge
  • Board for Correction of Military Records (BCMR) / Board for Correction of Naval Records (BCNR) available for any discharge, with no time limit; broader authority to correct records and grant relief on grounds of error or injustice
  • Special Discharge Review Programs (SDRP) certain programs exist specifically for veterans whose discharges were influenced by PTSD, MST, or TBI, or whose cases involve particular era-specific injustices

Grounds for Upgrade

The boards consider whether the discharge was proper (no procedural error) and equitable (fair given all the facts). Strong grounds for an upgrade often include:

  • PTSD, MST, or other mental health conditions that were undiagnosed or untreated at the time of the misconduct underlying the discharge
  • Brain injury or substance abuse disorder directly related to service
  • Systemic injustice or patterns of discrimination that influenced the discharge
  • Evidence that the punishment was disproportionate to the conduct at issue
  • Strong post-service record of rehabilitation, community contribution, or subsequent honorable service
For additional information, visit the official VA guide to military discharge upgrades and corrections

Our Approach to Discharge Upgrade Petitions

We begin with a thorough review of your DD214, service records, and separation documents to understand what happened and why. We then analyze which forum and which theory of relief gives the strongest path to an upgrade. The petition itself is built around a detailed personal statement, corroborating lay statements, medical or mental health evidence, and a legal argument that ties the evidence to the standard the board applies.

Discharge review petitions are not casual filings. A well-built submission significantly improves the odds of success. We take the time to do it right.

For a more detailed explanation of eligibility, evidence requirements and the review process, read our Military Discharge Upgrade Guide.

draft.title: Correcting Military Records
draft.excerpt: Errors in your DD214 or military service records can affect VA eligibility, employment, and more. We assist veterans in identifying errors and pursuing corrections through the appropriate administrative channels.
draft.body:
Why Military Records Matter

Your DD-214 (Certificate of Release or Discharge from Active Duty) is one of the most important documents you will have after military service. It establishes your service history, character of discharge, awards, occupational specialty, and more. Errors on the DD-214 , or in your underlying service records , can affect VA benefit eligibility, civil service preference, state veterans’ benefits, and employment.

Errors range from simple clerical mistakes (wrong dates, misspelled names, omitted awards) to substantive errors that mischaracterize service or exclude periods of active duty. The correction process depends on the nature and age of the error, and which military branch is involved.

Common Corrections We Assist With

  • Incorrect character of discharge or reason for discharge
  • Missing or incorrect service dates, component, or occupational specialty code
  • Omitted awards, decorations, or citations
  • Incorrect disability rating at separation through IDES/LDES process
  • Missing combat service designations or foreign service entries
  • Errors in narrative reason for separation that affect benefit eligibility
  • Upgrades to general or honorable discharge (overlaps with discharge upgrade petitions)

Correction Forums

The primary forum for correcting military records is the Board for Correction of Military Records (BCMR) for Army, Air Force, Space Force, and Coast Guard veterans, and the Board for Correction of Naval Records (BCNR) for Navy and Marine Corps veterans. These boards have broad authority to correct any military record when necessary to correct an error or remove an injustice.

For clerical errors that have no dispute about the underlying facts, a simpler request to the National Personnel Records Center (NPRC) or the relevant branch may suffice. We assess which avenue is most appropriate for your situation before investing time in the more extensive BCMR/BCNR petition process.

draft.title: TDIU / Unemployability
draft.excerpt: When service-connected disabilities prevent you from holding substantially gainful employment, VA can pay you at the 100% rate even if your combined rating is below 100%. We build TDIU claims grounded in vocational and medical evidence.
draft.body:
What Is TDIU?

Total Disability based on Individual Unemployability (TDIU) is a VA benefit that allows a veteran to receive compensation at the 100% rate even if their combined disability rating does not reach 100%. It is available when service-connected disabilities alone prevent the veteran from securing or maintaining substantially gainful employment , that is, work paying above the poverty threshold.

TDIU is one of the most significant benefits the VA offers. The difference between, say, a 70% combined rating and a 100% rating can mean several hundred dollars per month in additional compensation. For veterans who are genuinely unable to work because of their service-connected conditions, TDIU is often the correct and deserved outcome.

Eligibility Requirements

There are two paths to TDIU eligibility under the VA's schedular criteria:

  • Single disability at 60% or higher , one service-connected disability rated at 60% or more
  • Multiple disabilities at 70% combined , combined rating of 70% or higher, with at least one disability rated at 40% or more

Even if a veteran does not meet these thresholds, TDIU may still be granted on an extraschedular basis if the case is referred to the Director of Compensation and it is found that the veteran's disabilities render them unemployable. This is a narrower path but an important one for veterans whose situations do not fit neatly into the standard criteria.

What We Look At

A successful TDIU claim requires demonstrating two things: that the veteran's disabilities meet the rating threshold, and that those disabilities , not age, not unrelated conditions , are what prevent employment. We examine:

  • Current combined and individual disability ratings and whether increases are warranted before filing TDIU
  • Employment history and the nature of jobs held after service
  • Medical documentation of functional limitations directly tied to service-connected conditions
  • Lay statements from the veteran, family, and former employers or coworkers
  • Whether a VA vocational rehabilitation determination exists and how it bears on the claim
  • Marginal employment situations that do not constitute substantial gainful employment

Protecting an Existing TDIU Grant

If you are already receiving TDIU, the VA can propose to reduce or terminate it based on improvement in your condition or a finding that you have returned to substantially gainful employment. We also assist veterans in responding to proposed reductions and in protecting awards that have been in place for an extended period, which are subject to stricter procedural protections before they can be reduced.

draft.title: VA Disability Claims
draft.excerpt: Structured representation for initial claims, rating increases, secondary conditions, and AMA appeals , built around disciplined evidence and sound entitlement theory.
draft.body:
What Are VA Disability Claims?

A VA disability claim asks the Department of Veterans Affairs to recognize that a condition was caused or aggravated by military service and assign a disability rating , expressed as a percentage from 0% to 100% , that determines your monthly compensation. The combined rating drives the payment amount, and getting each condition properly rated matters enormously.

Claims can be filed for conditions that arose during service, were aggravated beyond their natural progression by service, or were caused by an already service-connected condition (secondary service connection). Presumptive conditions , those the VA automatically presumes are service-connected under certain circumstances , add another avenue that is often overlooked.

Types of Claims We Handle

  • Initial claims for veterans who have never filed or whose earlier claims were denied
  • Supplemental claims with new and relevant evidence to reopen prior denials
  • Increased rating claims when an existing condition has worsened
  • Secondary service connection for conditions caused or aggravated by a service-connected disability
  • Presumptive conditions, including those covered under the PACT Act for toxic exposure
  • Claims for Individual Unemployability (TDIU) when disabilities prevent substantial gainful employment
  • AMA appeals , Higher-Level Reviews and Board of Veterans' Appeals appeals under the new appeals system

Our Approach

Every claim starts with a thorough review of your service records, medical records, and any prior VA decisions. We identify the conditions that are service-connected or potentially service-connected, map the evidence needed to establish each element of entitlement, and build a submission designed to give the rater everything necessary to grant the claim at the correct rating.

Where evidence gaps exist , private medical opinions, nexus letters, buddy statements, or additional lay evidence , we identify what is needed and work with you to obtain it. We do not file claims speculatively; we file claims that are supported by theory and evidence.

The AMA Appeals Process

If the VA denies your claim or assigns a rating you believe is incorrect, you have one year from the decision date to choose an appeal lane under the Appeals Modernization Act:

  • Supplemental Claim: Submit new and relevant evidence for re-adjudication
  • Higher-Level Review: Request de novo review by a senior claims adjudicator , no new evidence, but errors in the prior decision can be corrected
  • Board of Veterans' Appeals: Direct appeal to a Veterans Law Judge, with or without a hearing, and with or without new evidence (Evidence Submission lane)

Choosing the right lane depends on what went wrong in the original decision. We analyze the rating decision, identify the specific error or missing evidence, and recommend the lane that gives the strongest path to a grant.

draft.title: VA C&P Exam vs. Private Medical Evidence: Which Carries More Weight?
draft.excerpt: A VA examiner does not automatically outrank your private doctor. When medical opinions conflict, the quality of the facts, reasoning, and analysis matters.
draft.body:
Does a VA C&P Examiner Automatically Outweigh a Private Doctor?

No. A medical opinion does not become more persuasive simply because it came from a VA examiner or a VA contractor. VA accepts private medical evidence, including medical records and privately completed Disability Benefits Questionnaires, as evidence in disability claims.

When a private clinician and a VA examiner disagree, the important issue is the quality of each opinion. The decision maker must consider whether the opinion is based on an accurate factual history, addresses the correct medical question, considers the relevant evidence, and explains the medical reasoning supporting its conclusion.

The name at the top of the examination is not the deciding factor. A detailed private opinion can be more persuasive than a weak C&P opinion, and a well-supported C&P opinion can be more persuasive than a conclusory private letter. The reasoning matters.

What Does VA Consider When Weighing Medical Opinions?

Medical opinions are not simply counted. Two negative opinions do not automatically beat one positive opinion. The real question is whether the opinion is competent, factually accurate, responsive to the issue, and supported by a medical explanation.

The Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims has repeatedly emphasized the importance of a reasoned analysis when medical professionals reach different conclusions. An opinion should allow the decision maker to understand both the conclusion and the medical basis for reaching it.

Record Review Matters, but It Is Not Everything

A provider should understand the relevant medical history. That may include service treatment records, post-service treatment, diagnostic testing, prior examinations, lay statements, and the veteran's reported history.

But merely writing that the claims file was reviewed does not transform a weak opinion into a strong one. The provider still has to identify the facts that matter and explain how those facts support the conclusion.

Likewise, a private provider's opinion should not be dismissed merely because that provider did not use VA's examination system. The question is whether the provider had sufficient information to offer an informed medical opinion.

Watch for an Inaccurate Factual Premise

An opinion can fall apart when the examiner bases the conclusion on facts that are not actually true. For example, an examiner may state that symptoms did not begin until years after service even though treatment records or credible statements document an earlier onset.

The same problem occurs when an examiner says there was no in-service event even though the service records document one, or says there is no diagnosis despite diagnostic evidence in the file.

When reviewing a negative C&P opinion, compare the examiner's factual summary against the actual record. A medical explanation built on the wrong facts may have limited value.

If you believe your examination overlooked important evidence or relied on inaccurate information, read our guide on What Makes a VA C&P Exam Inadequate? to understand other potential deficiencies and what they may mean for your claim.

Did the Examiner Address the Veteran's Lay Evidence?

Veterans can provide evidence about things they are capable of observing, including symptoms, when symptoms began, how frequently they occur, and how a disability affects daily life.

A medical examiner does not have to accept every statement without question. But an opinion can become problematic when the examiner ignores relevant lay evidence and bases a negative conclusion only on the absence of contemporaneous treatment records.

If the veteran reports that back pain began after an in-service injury and continued afterward, for example, the examiner should meaningfully address that history rather than simply stating that the service treatment records do not show chronic treatment.

Does the Opinion Actually Explain the Medical Reasoning?

This is often where the difference between two competing opinions becomes obvious.

Consider two opinions. One says, "The condition is less likely than not related to service because there is no evidence of chronicity." The other identifies the injury, discusses the veteran's subsequent symptoms, addresses imaging and treatment history, considers other risk factors, and explains medically why the current diagnosis is consistent with the claimed mechanism.

Those are not equivalent opinions simply because each contains a conclusion.

A useful medical rationale should connect the evidence to the conclusion. It should tell the reader why the medical facts support or do not support the claimed relationship.

What If the VA Examiner Says There Is No Medical Literature?

A statement that medical literature does not support a relationship should be examined carefully. Did the examiner identify the literature considered? Did the examiner explain how it applies to this veteran? Did the examiner address favorable studies submitted with the claim? Did the examiner discuss the veteran's particular medical history?

Medical literature can be important, but a claim involves an individual veteran. A generic statement about literature may not answer the actual medical question presented by the veteran's facts.

Secondary Claims Require the Right Question

Secondary service connection creates another common problem. Causation and aggravation are separate questions.

An examiner may conclude that a service-connected condition did not cause the claimed disability and stop there. If aggravation is reasonably raised, that may leave an important medical question unanswered.

A strong private opinion should make clear which theory it addresses. A negative VA opinion should be reviewed the same way. If the examiner answered only causation when aggravation was also at issue, the opinion may not fully resolve the claim.

What About a Private DBQ?

VA allows veterans to submit DBQs completed by private health care providers. A DBQ can document diagnoses, symptoms, functional impairment, range of motion, testing, and other findings relevant to the rating criteria.

VA may still determine that another examination is needed. If that happens, the private DBQ remains evidence in the record. The later C&P examination does not automatically erase or supersede it.

VA allows veterans to submit Disability Benefits Questionnaires (DBQs) completed by private health care providers, as explained in the VA's official guidance on Disability Benefits Questionnaires. A DBQ can document diagnoses, symptoms, functional impairment, range of motion, testing, and other findings relevant to the rating criteria.

When the Opinions Conflict, Read Both Closely

If a rating decision relies on a negative C&P opinion despite favorable private evidence, compare the opinions side by side.

  • Did each provider identify the correct diagnosis?
  • Did each provider understand the veteran's relevant history?
  • Did each opinion address the correct theory of service connection?
  • Did the examiner address favorable medical and lay evidence?
  • Is the conclusion based on accurate facts?
  • Did the provider explain the medical reasoning?
  • For a secondary claim, were both causation and aggravation addressed when applicable?

The answer to those questions can be much more important than whether the opinion was labeled "VA" or "private."

The Bottom Line

A C&P examiner does not automatically outrank a private medical provider. VA disability claims are decided on the evidence, and competing medical opinions should be evaluated based on their factual foundation, medical reasoning, and responsiveness to the issues in the claim.

If VA relies on a negative examination, read the examination itself. The real issue may not be that the examiner disagreed with your private doctor. The issue may be whether the examiner actually provided a better supported medical opinion.

If you're dealing with conflicting medical opinions, an unfavorable C&P examination, or a denied disability claim, VDA LLC can help you review the evidence and understand your options. Learn more about our disability claims and how we approach claims and appeals.

content.title: VA C&P Exam vs. Private Medical Evidence: Which Carries More Weight?
content.excerpt: A VA examiner does not automatically outrank your private doctor. When medical opinions conflict, the quality of the facts, reasoning, and analysis matters.
content.body:
Does a VA C&P Examiner Automatically Outweigh a Private Doctor?

No. A medical opinion does not become more persuasive simply because it came from a VA examiner or a VA contractor. VA accepts private medical evidence, including medical records and privately completed Disability Benefits Questionnaires, as evidence in disability claims.

When a private clinician and a VA examiner disagree, the important issue is the quality of each opinion. The decision maker must consider whether the opinion is based on an accurate factual history, addresses the correct medical question, considers the relevant evidence, and explains the medical reasoning supporting its conclusion.

The name at the top of the examination is not the deciding factor. A detailed private opinion can be more persuasive than a weak C&P opinion, and a well-supported C&P opinion can be more persuasive than a conclusory private letter. The reasoning matters.

What Does VA Consider When Weighing Medical Opinions?

Medical opinions are not simply counted. Two negative opinions do not automatically beat one positive opinion. The real question is whether the opinion is competent, factually accurate, responsive to the issue, and supported by a medical explanation.

The Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims has repeatedly emphasized the importance of a reasoned analysis when medical professionals reach different conclusions. An opinion should allow the decision maker to understand both the conclusion and the medical basis for reaching it.

Record Review Matters, but It Is Not Everything

A provider should understand the relevant medical history. That may include service treatment records, post-service treatment, diagnostic testing, prior examinations, lay statements, and the veteran's reported history.

But merely writing that the claims file was reviewed does not transform a weak opinion into a strong one. The provider still has to identify the facts that matter and explain how those facts support the conclusion.

Likewise, a private provider's opinion should not be dismissed merely because that provider did not use VA's examination system. The question is whether the provider had sufficient information to offer an informed medical opinion.

Watch for an Inaccurate Factual Premise

An opinion can fall apart when the examiner bases the conclusion on facts that are not actually true. For example, an examiner may state that symptoms did not begin until years after service even though treatment records or credible statements document an earlier onset.

The same problem occurs when an examiner says there was no in-service event even though the service records document one, or says there is no diagnosis despite diagnostic evidence in the file.

When reviewing a negative C&P opinion, compare the examiner's factual summary against the actual record. A medical explanation built on the wrong facts may have limited value.

Did the Examiner Address the Veteran's Lay Evidence?

Veterans can provide evidence about things they are capable of observing, including symptoms, when symptoms began, how frequently they occur, and how a disability affects daily life.

A medical examiner does not have to accept every statement without question. But an opinion can become problematic when the examiner ignores relevant lay evidence and bases a negative conclusion only on the absence of contemporaneous treatment records.

If the veteran reports that back pain began after an in-service injury and continued afterward, for example, the examiner should meaningfully address that history rather than simply stating that the service treatment records do not show chronic treatment.

This is often where the difference between two competing opinions becomes obvious.

The other identifies the injury, discusses the veteran's subsequent symptoms, addresses imaging and treatment history, considers other risk factors, and explains medically why the current diagnosis is consistent with the claimed mechanism.

Those are not equivalent opinions simply because each contains a conclusion.

A useful medical rationale should connect the evidence to the conclusion. It should tell the reader why the medical facts support or do not support the claimed relationship.

What If the VA Examiner Says There Is No Medical Literature?

A statement that medical literature does not support a relationship should be examined carefully. Did the examiner identify the literature considered? Did the examiner explain how it applies to this veteran? Did the examiner address favorable studies submitted with the claim? Did the examiner discuss the veteran's particular medical history?

Medical literature can be important, but a claim involves an individual veteran. A generic statement about literature may not answer the actual medical question presented by the veteran's facts.

VA allows veterans to submit DBQs completed by private health care providers. A DBQ can document diagnoses, symptoms, functional impairment, range of motion, testing, and other findings relevant to the rating criteria.

VA may still determine that another examination is needed. If that happens, the private DBQ remains evidence in the record. The later C&P examination does not automatically erase or supersede it.

When the Opinions Conflict, Read Both Closely

If a rating decision relies on a negative C&P opinion despite favorable private evidence, compare the opinions side by side.

  • Did each provider identify the correct diagnosis?
  • Did each provider understand the veteran's relevant history?
  • Did each opinion address the correct theory of service connection?
  • Did the examiner address favorable medical and lay evidence?
  • Is the conclusion based on accurate facts?
  • Did the provider explain the medical reasoning?
  • For a secondary claim, were both causation and aggravation addressed when applicable?

The answer to those questions can be much more important than whether the opinion was labeled "VA" or "private."

The Bottom Line

A C&P examiner does not automatically outrank a private medical provider. VA disability claims are decided on the evidence, and competing medical opinions should be evaluated based on their factual foundation, medical reasoning, and responsiveness to the issues in the claim.

draft.title: Clear and Unmistakable Error (CUE) in VA Decisions: A Practical Guide
draft.excerpt: CUE is not a second chance to reweigh evidence. Understand the demanding legal standard, finality, and how to identify a specific outcome-changing error.
draft.body:
CUE is not a second chance to reweigh evidence. Understand the demanding legal standard, finality, and how to identify a specific outcome-changing error. The outcome of a VA disability claim depends on the specific evidence, the governing regulation, and the procedural history. This guide explains the practical questions to examine before deciding what to file.

Why CUE is different from an ordinary appeal

Clear and unmistakable error is a narrow way to seek revision of a final VA decision. It is not a general complaint that the earlier rater made a poor judgment call. The claimant must identify an error of fact or law based on the record and law applicable at the time, and explain why the result would have been manifestly different without that error.

For final agency decisions, 38 C.F.R. § 3.105(a) governs revision based on CUE. Board decisions have separate CUE procedures under 38 U.S.C. § 7111 and 38 C.F.R. Part 20. Confusing those pathways can derail an otherwise serious allegation.

Three elements of a meaningful CUE theory

First, identify the precise factual or legal mistake. Second, establish that the error is undebatable under the law and record then existing, not simply one reasonable interpretation among several. Third, show that correcting the error would necessarily have changed the outcome. An error that would only have triggered additional development generally does not satisfy this demanding standard.

A statement that 'VA should have rated me higher' is not enough. A stronger allegation identifies the specific diagnostic code, evidence then before VA, the applicable regulation, and the outcome compelled by those facts.

Why a failure in the duty to assist usually is not CUE

An incomplete record can support a timely appeal or a duty-to-assist challenge, but failure to obtain an examination or records generally is not CUE. The reason is that missing development does not establish what the missing evidence would have shown. CUE review does not ordinarily permit constructing a better record with later medical evidence.

Similarly, disagreement over how VA weighed competing medical opinions is usually not CUE. If reasonable adjudicators could reach different conclusions from the record, the error is not undebatable.

Practical takeaway: Before choosing a review option or submitting more evidence, compare the rating decision with the records VA actually considered. The most useful next step addresses the precise missing legal or factual element.$

A failure to obtain necessary records or provide an adequate examination may instead raise a duty-to-assist issue. For a closer look at these situations, read our guide to VA Duty to Assist Errors and how they can affect disability claims and appeals.

Historical law matters

A 2010 rating decision must be analyzed using the law and evidence applicable to that 2010 decision. Applying a modern rating criterion retroactively without legal authority can produce an invalid theory. Changes in presumptions, diagnostic codes, and interpretations may affect current claims without proving that a decades-old final decision was unmistakably erroneous.

Before drafting, retrieve the complete rating decision, evidence list, service records, and the historical version of the relevant regulation. The exact decision date can determine whether a particular legal provision applied.

Examples of potentially stronger and weaker arguments

Potentially stronger: a final decision expressly acknowledges an undisputed fact and then applies a regulation that plainly excludes that fact, with only one legally possible result. Potentially weaker: an examiner failed to discuss symptoms, the rater preferred a VA opinion over a private opinion, or the veteran now has a more persuasive nexus letter. The latter issues may justify another procedural route, but not necessarily CUE.

A favorable finding made in a later decision is not automatically proof that an older final decision contained CUE. Each decision has its own record and applicable law.

How to present a focused CUE request

Identify the exact final decision and issue, quote or accurately summarize the rule that was in force, identify the evidence already in the file, and explain the manifestly different outcome. Avoid stacking unrelated theories into one vague paragraph. If an earlier decision is still within an appeal window, an ordinary decision-review option may be more appropriate than a collateral CUE attack.

Effective dates and revision consequences can be significant, which is why CUE arguments deserve especially careful review by a qualified accredited representative.

Not every unfavorable VA decision requires a CUE request. If the decision is still within the applicable review period, a Higher-Level Review or Supplemental Claim may be more appropriate. Our guide to Higher-Level Review vs. Supplemental Claim explains how these options differ.

Questions to ask before you file

  • What exactly did VA concede in its favorable findings, and what element remains disputed?
  • Which evidence was already in the record when VA made the decision?
  • Is the issue a legal or factual mistake, missing development, or a genuine lack of supporting evidence?
  • What is the date of the decision notice, and which review deadline applies?
  • Would the proposed evidence answer the specific reason VA gave for its decision?

Official rules and further reading

The primary authorities and VA guidance below provide a starting point. Regulations and interpretations can change, and the law applicable to an older decision may differ from the law currently in effect.

  • ecfr.gov/current/title-38/chapter-I/part-3/section-3.105
  • ecfr.gov/current/title-38/chapter-I/part-20/subpart-O

draft.title: Higher-Level Review vs. Supplemental Claim: Which VA Appeal Fits Your Case?
draft.excerpt: Choosing the wrong review lane can waste months. Learn how to distinguish a record-based error from a case that needs new and relevant evidence.
draft.body:
Choosing the wrong review lane can waste months. Learn how to distinguish a record-based error from a case that needs new and relevant evidence. The outcome of a VA disability claim depends on the specific evidence, the governing regulation, and the procedural history. This guide explains the practical questions to examine before deciding what to file.

Start with the actual reason VA denied the claim

A decision review is not simply a request for VA to look again. The question is what was wrong with the prior decision and what kind of review can legally correct it. Read the evidence list, favorable findings, reasons for denial, and notice date. If VA ignored favorable evidence already in the file, an error-focused review may be appropriate. If the file lacked a competent medical link, an evidence-building review is usually the better fit.

A favorable finding that a veteran has a current diagnosis does not necessarily establish the in-service event or the medical relationship to service. Separating these elements avoids appealing the wrong issue. Identify each contested issue by the decision date, because different conditions in the same decision can call for different strategies.

What Higher-Level Review can and cannot do

A Higher-Level Review, requested on VA Form 20-0996, asks a senior adjudicator to review the evidence that was before the earlier decision-maker. It does not permit new evidence. A written argument pointing to documents already in the record is different from introducing a new medical report. The reviewer can correct factual or legal mistakes, disagree with the earlier evaluation, or identify a pre-decisional duty-to-assist error.

A common misconception is that every Higher-Level Review must allege clear and unmistakable error. It does not. CUE is a distinct, demanding standard for revising certain final decisions; ordinary Higher-Level Review can address other errors and differences of opinion. An informal conference is optional and is meant to identify errors, not supply new evidence. It may add time.

For a more detailed explanation of this distinction, read our guide to Clear and Unmistakable Error (CUE) in VA Decisions, including why the legal standard differs from an ordinary review of a VA decision.

When a Supplemental Claim makes more sense

A Supplemental Claim, generally filed on VA Form 20-0995, is designed for new and relevant evidence. New means not previously part of the actual record; relevant means tending to prove or disprove a matter at issue. A private nexus opinion addressing a deficient VA examination, missing treatment records, or a detailed witness statement can change the evidentiary picture.

The new evidence must address the actual reason for denial. Another copy of an already-considered diagnosis may add nothing if VA accepted the diagnosis but denied the causal link. A clinician's opinion should identify the relevant medical history, explain the reasoning, and address contrary evidence rather than merely state that a disability is 'related to service.'

Practical takeaway: Before choosing a review option or submitting more evidence, compare the rating decision with the records VA actually considered. The most useful next step addresses the precise missing legal or factual element.

Deadlines and preserving the effective date

For most modern VA compensation decisions, seeking an eligible review option within one year can maintain continuous pursuit under 38 C.F.R. § 3.2500, subject to the rules governing the sequence of review options. A Supplemental Claim can also be filed after a year, but the effective-date consequences can be substantial. Do not assume that filing years later automatically preserves the date of the first claim.

A Higher-Level Review is generally available after an initial or Supplemental Claim decision, not as an immediate repeat HLR of the same issue. Following an HLR decision, a Supplemental Claim or Board appeal may be available. The correct sequence matters. Read the decision notice and preserve proof of timely filing.

A practical decision example

Suppose VA denied service connection because the examiner claimed there was no in-service injury, even though the service treatment record documenting that injury was in the file. An HLR can focus on that factual mistake and the examiner's inaccurate premise. By contrast, if VA acknowledged the injury and diagnosis but found no medical nexus, a new well-supported medical opinion may make a Supplemental Claim more productive.

Sometimes the decision contains both problems: a missing examination and inadequate evidence of the relationship. A representative should identify what existed before the decision, what VA should have developed, and what additional evidence is now available. There is no universal best appeal lane.

When VA fails to obtain required evidence or relies on an inadequate examination, the problem may involve a pre-decisional duty-to-assist error. Our guide to VA Duty to Assist Errors explains how these issues can affect claims and decision reviews.

How to prepare a focused review

Build a one-page issue chart identifying the condition, decision date, favorable findings, disputed element, and supporting evidence. For HLR, cite the existing record precisely: examination date, treatment note, personnel record, or regulation. For a Supplemental Claim, identify what evidence is genuinely new and explain how it resolves the gap. Keep separate claims and issues clearly identified.

Do not overlook the Board of Veterans' Appeals. Its Direct Review, Evidence Submission, and Hearing dockets have different evidence rules. Choosing between them can be as consequential as choosing between HLR and Supplemental Claim.

Choosing the appropriate review option depends on the evidence, the reason for the previous decision and the applicable deadlines. If you need help evaluating your options, learn more about VDA LLC's VA disability claims and appeals assistance.

Questions to ask before you file

  • What exactly did VA concede in its favorable findings, and what element remains disputed?
  • Which evidence was already in the record when VA made the decision?
  • Is the issue a legal or factual mistake, missing development, or a genuine lack of supporting evidence?
  • What is the date of the decision notice, and which review deadline applies?
  • Would the proposed evidence answer the specific reason VA gave for its decision?

Official rules and further reading

The primary authorities and VA guidance below provide a starting point. Regulations and interpretations can change, and the law applicable to an older decision may differ from the law currently in effect.

Separating these elements avoids appealing the wrong issue. Identify each contested issue by the decision date, because different conditions in the same decision can call for different strategies.

draft.excerpt: VA must make reasonable efforts to obtain certain evidence and provide examinations when required. Learn how to identify a genuine pre-decisional development error.
draft.body:
VA must make reasonable efforts to obtain certain evidence and provide examinations when required. Learn how to identify a genuine pre-decisional development error. The outcome of a VA disability claim depends on the specific evidence, the governing regulation, and the procedural history. This guide explains the practical questions to examine before deciding what to file.

What the duty to assist actually requires

VA's duty to assist is a legal obligation, not a promise that every claim will be granted. Under 38 U.S.C. § 5103A and 38 C.F.R. § 3.159, VA generally must make reasonable efforts to obtain relevant records and provide a medical examination or opinion when the statutory criteria are met. The precise duties depend on the type of claim, the information provided, and the record already available.

The important distinction is between evidence VA had a duty to seek and evidence that would merely have been helpful. VA is not required to order an examination in every claim, and a veteran's disagreement with a medical conclusion is not by itself proof of a duty-to-assist error.

Missing service and federal records

Service treatment records, relevant personnel records, and identified federal medical records can establish an in-service event or show symptoms long before a civilian diagnosis. If VA made a decision without adequately pursuing relevant federal records, the development may be deficient. A veteran should identify the unit, installation, approximate dates, treatment facility, or deployment involved.

If records cannot be located, VA has notice obligations. An absence of documentation in an incomplete file should not be treated as conclusive proof that an event never occurred. At the same time, missing records do not automatically establish the claimed event or medical nexus.

Private records and the veteran’s role

VA can help request private treatment records when the veteran identifies the provider and provides required authorization, often on VA Forms 21-4142 and 21-4142a. Incomplete provider information or missing authorization can prevent a request. Keep copies of records yourself where possible, and identify why each provider's records matter.

A private physician's record may document years of symptoms, a diagnosis, or treatment soon after discharge. The value lies in its relevance to the denied element, not simply the number of pages submitted.

Practical takeaway: Before choosing a review option or submitting more evidence, compare the rating decision with the records VA actually considered. The most useful next step addresses the precise missing legal or factual element.

When an examination or medical opinion is required

For an original service-connection claim, the examination threshold considers evidence of current disability or persistent symptoms, evidence establishing a relevant service event, an indication the condition may be associated with service, and whether the file otherwise contains sufficient medical evidence. This is not the same as already proving the claim. Credible lay evidence can matter, depending on the facts.

If an exam is provided, adequacy matters. An opinion that ignores material medical history, relies on an inaccurate factual premise, or supplies no understandable reasoning may require correction. But a negative opinion is not automatically inadequate merely because it is unfavorable.

If VA obtained an examination but the examiner overlooked important evidence, relied on inaccurate facts, or failed to explain their medical reasoning, the examination itself may be inadequate. Read our guide on What Makes a VA C&P Exam Inadequate? for a closer look at these issues.

What happens after an HLR finds a pre-decisional error

A Higher-Level Review can identify a duty-to-assist error that existed before the decision being reviewed. VA typically closes the HLR issue and establishes a separate process to obtain the missing evidence, such as records or a new examination, before issuing a new decision. This is a development correction, not an award of benefits.

The veteran should attend requested examinations, verify contact information, and monitor for notices. A correction can still result in a denial if the completed evidence does not support entitlement.

A duty-to-assist error is one possible outcome of a Higher-Level Review, but it is important to understand whether this review option is appropriate for your claim in the first place. Our guide to Higher-Level Review vs. Supplemental Claim explains the differences in evidence requirements, review procedures, and filing deadlines.

How to articulate the error precisely

A useful argument names the missing action and why the record triggered it: 'The service records documented repeated ankle complaints, the claim identified ongoing ankle pain, and VA denied without obtaining a medical examination or opinion.' Compare that with a vague statement that 'VA failed its duty to assist.' Specificity gives the reviewer a concrete record-based issue to resolve.

Review the decision date carefully. Evidence created after that decision ordinarily cannot establish that VA committed a pre-decisional duty-to-assist error by failing to consider it. Later evidence may instead support a Supplemental Claim.

Identifying a duty-to-assist error requires careful review of the evidence, the original decision, and VA's obligations at the time. If you need help understanding a denial or evaluating your available review options, learn more about VDA LLC's VA disability claims and appeals assistance.

Questions to ask before you file

  • What exactly did VA concede in its favorable findings, and what element remains disputed?
  • Which evidence was already in the record when VA made the decision?
  • Is the issue a legal or factual mistake, missing development, or a genuine lack of supporting evidence?
  • What is the date of the decision notice, and which review deadline applies?
  • Would the proposed evidence answer the specific reason VA gave for its decision?

Official rules and further reading

The primary authorities and VA guidance below provide a starting point. Regulations and interpretations can change, and the law applicable to an older decision may differ from the law currently in effect.

content.title: VA Duty to Assist Errors: When VA Fails to Develop Your Claim
content.excerpt: VA must make reasonable efforts to obtain certain evidence and provide examinations when required. Learn how to identify a genuine pre-decisional development error.
content.body:
VA must make reasonable efforts to obtain certain evidence and provide examinations when required. Learn how to identify a genuine pre-decisional development error. The outcome of a VA disability claim depends on the specific evidence, the governing regulation, and the procedural history. This guide explains the practical questions to examine before deciding what to file.

What the duty to assist actually requires

VA's duty to assist is a legal obligation, not a promise that every claim will be granted. Under 38 U.S.C. § 5103A and 38 C.F.R. § 3.159, VA generally must make reasonable efforts to obtain relevant records and provide a medical examination or opinion when the statutory criteria are met. The precise duties depend on the type of claim, the information provided, and the record already available.

The important distinction is between evidence VA had a duty to seek and evidence that would merely have been helpful. VA is not required to order an examination in every claim, and a veteran's disagreement with a medical conclusion is not by itself proof of a duty-to-assist error.

Missing service and federal records

Service treatment records, relevant personnel records, and identified federal medical records can establish an in-service event or show symptoms long before a civilian diagnosis. If VA made a decision without adequately pursuing relevant federal records, the development may be deficient. A veteran should identify the unit, installation, approximate dates, treatment facility, or deployment involved.

If records cannot be located, VA has notice obligations. An absence of documentation in an incomplete file should not be treated as conclusive proof that an event never occurred. At the same time, missing records do not automatically establish the claimed event or medical nexus.

Private records and the veteran’s role

VA can help request private treatment records when the veteran identifies the provider and provides required authorization, often on VA Forms 21-4142 and 21-4142a. Incomplete provider information or missing authorization can prevent a request. Keep copies of records yourself where possible, and identify why each provider's records matter.

A private physician's record may document years of symptoms, a diagnosis, or treatment soon after discharge. The value lies in its relevance to the denied element, not simply the number of pages submitted.

Practical takeaway: Before choosing a review option or submitting more evidence, compare the rating decision with the records VA actually considered. The most useful next step addresses the precise missing legal or factual element.

When an examination or medical opinion is required

For an original service-connection claim, the examination threshold considers evidence of current disability or persistent symptoms, evidence establishing a relevant service event, an indication the condition may be associated with service, and whether the file otherwise contains sufficient medical evidence. This is not the same as already proving the claim. Credible lay evidence can matter, depending on the facts.

If an exam is provided, adequacy matters. An opinion that ignores material medical history, relies on an inaccurate factual premise, or supplies no understandable reasoning may require correction. But a negative opinion is not automatically inadequate merely because it is unfavorable.

What happens after an HLR finds a pre-decisional error

A Higher-Level Review can identify a duty-to-assist error that existed before the decision being reviewed. VA typically closes the HLR issue and establishes a separate process to obtain the missing evidence, such as records or a new examination, before issuing a new decision. This is a development correction, not an award of benefits.

The veteran should attend requested examinations, verify contact information, and monitor for notices. A correction can still result in a denial if the completed evidence does not support entitlement.

How to articulate the error precisely

A useful argument names the missing action and why the record triggered it: 'The service records documented repeated ankle complaints, the claim identified ongoing ankle pain, and VA denied without obtaining a medical examination or opinion.' Compare that with a vague statement that 'VA failed its duty to assist.' Specificity gives the reviewer a concrete record-based issue to resolve.

Review the decision date carefully. Evidence created after that decision ordinarily cannot establish that VA committed a pre-decisional duty-to-assist error by failing to consider it. Later evidence may instead support a Supplemental Claim.

Questions to ask before you file

  • What exactly did VA concede in its favorable findings, and what element remains disputed?
  • Which evidence was already in the record when VA made the decision?
  • Is the issue a legal or factual mistake, missing development, or a genuine lack of supporting evidence?
  • What is the date of the decision notice, and which review deadline applies?
  • Would the proposed evidence answer the specific reason VA gave for its decision?

Official rules and further reading

The primary authorities and VA guidance below provide a starting point. Regulations and interpretations can change, and the law applicable to an older decision may differ from the law currently in effect.

draft.title: VA Claim Denied? Your Three Appeal Options Under the AMA
draft.excerpt: A denial letter doesn’t end the fight. The Appeals Modernization Act created three distinct lanes for challenging a VA decision , and which one you choose can make the difference between a grant and another denial.
draft.body:
Reading the Rating Decision First

Before choosing an appeal lane, read the rating decision carefully. The VA is required to provide “reasons and bases” for its decision , a written explanation of what evidence it considered and why it reached the conclusion it did. That explanation tells you what went wrong and, consequently, which appeal path addresses it.

Common reasons for denial include: no nexus established between the current condition and military service, no current diagnosis on record, a favorable nexus opinion outweighed by a negative VA examination, or a condition found not to have been incurred in service. Each of these requires a different fix, and the AMA lanes are designed around that distinction.

The one-year rule: You have one year from the date of the rating decision to file an appeal in any AMA lane without losing your effective date. Missing this window doesn’t bar you from appealing, but it will affect how far back your benefits can be paid.

Lane 1: Supplemental Claim

A Supplemental Claim is the right choice when you have new and relevant evidence that was not before the VA when it made the original decision. “New” means the evidence wasn’t previously part of the record. “Relevant” means it could reasonably affect the outcome , either by tending to prove or disprove an element of the claim.

Common new evidence in a Supplemental Claim includes a private medical nexus opinion, buddy statements from fellow service members, treatment records from a private provider, or a more detailed lay statement from the veteran explaining the in-service event. The duty to assist remains active in the Supplemental Claim lane, meaning the VA must help develop the claim if asked.

Supplemental Claims are generally faster than BVA appeals, and they carry a real advantage: if granted, they preserve the original effective date from your initial claim filing date.

Lane 2: Higher-Level Review

A Higher-Level Review (HLR) asks a more senior VA adjudicator to review your file for errors without submitting new evidence. You cannot introduce new evidence in an HLR , the senior reviewer is looking at exactly what the original rater considered. What they’re looking for is clear and unmistakable error: a situation where the rater misapplied the law, overlooked an element of entitlement, or made a factual error that is obvious from the existing record.

HLR is the right lane when the evidence is strong but the rater made a legal or procedural mistake. It is not the right lane when the record simply needs more evidence to be persuasive. If a medical nexus was never established, HLR won’t fix it , a Supplemental Claim or BVA appeal with new evidence will.

One important feature of HLR: you can request a phone conference with the senior adjudicator to identify the specific error in the decision. Not all adjudicators take these calls, and not all errors are correctable at the HLR level, but the option is worth knowing about.

If you're unsure whether your claim requires new evidence or a review of an existing decision, our guide to Higher-Level Review vs. Supplemental Claim explains the key differences and when each option may be appropriate.

Lane 3: Board of Veterans’ Appeals

A BVA appeal goes directly to a Veterans Law Judge and offers the most thorough review of the three lanes. At the BVA, you have three options for how the appeal proceeds:

  • Direct Review: The judge reviews the existing record and makes a decision without new evidence or a hearing
  • Evidence Submission: You may submit new evidence (within 90 days of filing the Notice of Disagreement), but there is no hearing
  • Hearing: You or your representative appears before a Veterans Law Judge, and you may also submit additional evidence

BVA appeals take significantly longer than the other two lanes , often 18 to 36 months or more at current docket volumes , but they offer the highest level of legal scrutiny and access to the CAVC (Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims) if the BVA denies the claim. For complex cases involving legal interpretation, the BVA hearing lane is often the strongest path.

Choosing the Right Lane

The choice comes down to what went wrong. If the record is complete but the rater made an error, HLR is fast and efficient. If the record needs more evidence , a nexus opinion, treatment records, a lay statement , the Supplemental Claim lane develops the claim with the duty to assist intact. If the case is legally complex, involves a large retroactive award, or has already been through the other lanes, BVA is likely the right destination.

It is also possible to pursue more than one lane, with important restrictions: you cannot have a Supplemental Claim and an HLR pending on the same issue at the same time, and filing a BVA appeal closes the other lanes for that issue during the pendency of the appeal. Understanding the sequencing matters as much as understanding the lanes themselves.

If your VA disability claim has been denied, understanding the reason for that decision is the first step towards choosing an appropriate review option. VDA LLC provides VA disability claims and appeals assistance, helping veterans evaluate decisions, review evidence and navigate available appeal procedures.

draft.title: Secondary Service Connection: Connecting a New Condition to a VA Disability
draft.excerpt: A disability can qualify when a service-connected condition causes or aggravates it. Learn the evidence VA evaluates under 38 C.F.R. § 3.310.
draft.body:
A disability can qualify when a service-connected condition causes or aggravates it. Learn the evidence VA evaluates under 38 C.F.R. § 3.310. The outcome of a VA disability claim depends on the specific evidence, the governing regulation, and the procedural history. This guide explains the practical questions to examine before deciding what to file.

The two paths: causation and aggravation

Secondary service connection recognizes that a disability can result from another condition VA has already service connected. Under 38 C.F.R. § 3.310, the question may be whether the primary disability caused the new condition or whether it aggravated the new condition beyond its natural progression. Those are distinct medical theories and should not be treated as interchangeable.

For example, a service-connected orthopedic injury might alter gait and contribute to another joint problem. A clinician should explain the mechanism and the particular veteran's medical history rather than simply assert that one diagnosis commonly accompanies another.

The evidence you need

The record ordinarily must establish a current secondary disability, an already service-connected primary condition, and a competent link between them. The link may come from medical literature, clinical records, a reasoned medical opinion, or a combination of evidence. Medical articles alone seldom establish the relationship in an individual case without explanation of how the research applies.

Lay statements can establish observable symptoms, onset, and changes in function. They usually cannot replace a specialized medical explanation when causation involves complex physiology.

A well-supported medical nexus opinion can help explain the relationship between an existing service-connected condition and a secondary disability. Our guide to VA Nexus Letters explains what medical opinions should contain and how they can support a disability claim.

Aggravation is not the same as causation

A condition can predate the primary disability and still be aggravated by it. Under the aggravation provisions of § 3.310, VA considers baseline severity and the degree of additional disability attributable to the service-connected condition. Records from before the worsening and during the worsening can be especially useful.

draft.title: VA Denied Your Claim for Lack of Medical Nexus: What Next?
draft.excerpt: A current diagnosis and an in-service event do not always establish service connection. Learn how to identify the missing medical link and respond strategically.
draft.body:
A current diagnosis and an in-service event do not always establish service connection. Learn how to identify the missing medical link and respond strategically. The outcome of a VA disability claim depends on the specific evidence, the governing regulation, and the procedural history. This guide explains the practical questions to examine before deciding what to file.

What a medical nexus actually establishes

For many direct service-connection claims, VA must find a current disability, a qualifying in-service disease, injury, or event, and a relationship between the two. That relationship is often called the medical nexus. A veteran may have extensive treatment records proving the current diagnosis and still be denied if the evidence does not connect it to service.

Read the favorable findings before responding. If VA already conceded the current disability and an in-service event, the dispute may be much narrower than the denial letter initially suggests.

Why a bare conclusion is weak evidence

An opinion stating only that a condition 'is at least as likely as not related to service' may be less persuasive if it does not explain why. A useful opinion identifies the relevant medical facts, onset and course of symptoms, exposure or injury, applicable medical principles, and why alternative explanations are more or less likely.

A clinician need not use magic words to be persuasive. What matters is whether the reasoning permits the adjudicator to understand the conclusion and evaluate it against contrary evidence.

A detailed medical opinion can be particularly valuable when VA has denied a claim because the evidence does not establish a connection to service. Our guide to VA Nexus Letters explains what makes a persuasive medical opinion, what supporting evidence may be relevant, and why a letter alone does not guarantee approval.

Review the VA examiner’s factual assumptions

Some negative opinions rest on an assertion that no relevant event occurred, no symptoms were reported, or no treatment happened for many years. Compare those assertions against the actual service records, personnel history, lay statements, and post-service records. An opinion built on a materially inaccurate factual premise may have reduced probative value.

A gap in treatment can be relevant, but it is not automatically dispositive. The examiner should consider competent reports of symptoms and explain their medical significance rather than substitute silence in the records for a complete analysis.

Practical takeaway: Before choosing a review option or submitting more evidence, compare the rating decision with the records VA actually considered. The most useful next step addresses the precise missing legal or factual element.

When a VA examiner's conclusions conflict with medical evidence from a private clinician, the issue is not simply which opinion came first or who performed the examination. Read our guide to VA C&P Exams vs. Private Medical Evidence to understand how competing medical opinions may be evaluated.

Choose the review lane that matches the deficiency

If the examiner ignored evidence already in the record or VA failed to obtain a necessary opinion, a Higher-Level Review may be appropriate to identify an error based on the prior record. If the claim genuinely needs a new medical nexus opinion, a Supplemental Claim with new and relevant evidence may be more effective. The two approaches solve different problems.

Preserve applicable one-year review deadlines when possible. A late Supplemental Claim can still be available, but the potential effective date may change.

Choosing between these review options depends on whether the previous decision contained an error that can be addressed using the existing record or whether new evidence is needed. Our guide to Higher-Level Review vs. Supplemental Claim explains the differences, including evidence requirements and filing deadlines.

Direct, secondary, and presumptive theories differ

A nexus dispute can arise under direct service connection, secondary service connection, or a presumptive theory. Under 38 C.F.R. § 3.310, a secondary opinion may need to address both causation and aggravation. For a qualifying presumptive condition, the law may supply the connection when the required service and diagnosis criteria are met. Do not demand a traditional nexus opinion for a presumption that removes that requirement.

The correct theory depends on the veteran's service, diagnosis, and evidence. Multiple theories may be reasonably raised, but each should be analyzed on its own terms.

Build the record around the denied element

A focused submission can include a detailed chronology, medical records, competent lay statements, deployment or personnel documentation, and a well-reasoned opinion addressing the prior denial. Ask the clinician to review the specific unfavorable examination and explain any disagreement with its factual or medical assumptions.

More paperwork is not automatically better evidence. The objective is to resolve the precise uncertainty that caused the denial while keeping the procedural history and effective date intact.

Questions to ask before you file

  • What exactly did VA concede in its favorable findings, and what element remains disputed?
  • Which evidence was already in the record when VA made the decision?
  • Is the issue a legal or factual mistake, missing development, or a genuine lack of supporting evidence?
  • What is the date of the decision notice, and which review deadline applies?
  • Would the proposed evidence answer the specific reason VA gave for its decision?
A denial based on lack of medical nexus can involve conflicting medical opinions, incomplete evidence or an incorrectly applied service-connection standard.
